name: default
_about: The default avatar: a 16x16 slime, drawn in two inks. '#' is the body and 'o' is everything on it -- eyes, mouth, and the highlight on the top-left of the dome -- so the art assumes throughout that 'o' is the *lighter* of the two. A theme that inverts that relationship turns the highlight into a scuff mark. Every sprite shares these inks: the thought bubble is a '#' cloud with 'o' dots, the muted bubble a '#' bubble with an 'o' cross, so a theme reaches all of them at once and there is nothing to keep in step by hand.
_palette: Palette keys are the single characters used in the .txt frames; '.' is always transparent and may not appear here. Colours are #rrggbb or #rrggbbaa. '*' is the only translucent ink: over body cells it composites to the one grey in the avatar, and think.txt uses it for a glint. This block is the *base* palette: it declares which characters exist, and every theme below is merged over it, so a new ink added here appears in every theme at this colour until one tints it.
_custom_inks: M1c.5. Which inks the derived-colour theme drives when the user picks a body colour in Settings. 'body' is what the picker sets; 'feature' is derived as the true complement of it, lifted in lightness only as far as it must be to stay distinguishable, and never made darker than the body because it is the gloss on the dome as well as the eyes; 'translucent' names the inks that take the feature's colour at their own alpha. These are the defaults, written out so the rule is visible in the art rather than only in the code -- an avatar drawn with different letters states its own here and the picker follows. The derived palette is merged over the base 'palette' block above, exactly as a named theme is, so it depends only on the colour picked and not on which theme was loaded when the picker was opened. It is stored in settings.json, never here: the picker and a hand edit of this file therefore cannot overwrite each other.
_themes:
M1c.4. Named palette variants, in picker order; each one states only the inks it changes. Chosen in Settings (the cog), stored per avatar in settings.json, and settable by name from code -- AvatarSource::set_theme. Changing one costs a reload of this directory, which is the same path a hot edit takes, so tuning a colour here shows up as soon as the file is saved.

The brief these were drawn to: the mono slime reads as a hole in a dark desktop, and the black thought bubble beside it is close to invisible. The lever is the body ink, and the answer is a *mid-tone*: a body far enough above the desktop's black to be a shape, and far enough below 'o' that white eyes still read on it. Mid-tones are also the only values that survive the widget being dragged onto a bright wallpaper, since black and white each vanish on one of them.

themes.name: mono
themes._about: What shipped before themes existed: black body, white features. Kept because it is the register the art was drawn in, and because on a mid-grey desktop it is still the sharpest of the four.

themes.name: jade
themes._about: The classic coloured slime -- one saturated mid-tone body, white features, unchanged composition. The most conservative of the three: it changes nothing about how the character reads, only that it is now a shape rather than an absence.

themes.name: ember
themes._about: A warm duotone: the white ink goes too, replaced by a pale gold, so the character is built out of two hues rather than a hue and white. Reads hotter and more arcade than jade, and the gold keeps its contrast against the body without ever being as bright as paper.

themes.name: jelly
themes._about: The one that takes the word slime literally: the body ink is translucent, so the desktop shows faintly through it and the character is made of the same stuff a jelly is. The only theme that uses the format's alpha. The gloss is pushed to a near-opaque white so there is still one hard specular on a body that is otherwise soft.

_anchors: Cells on the character that accessories hang off, so the art and the placements agree by name instead of by number. head_top is deliberately unused: the band is 260 px, which at scale 16 is exactly the 16 cells the body already fills, so anything placed above row 0 enlarges the envelope and the whole avatar is scaled down to fit it -- one cell above the head costs 16 px off the body. There is horizontal slack, so accessories go beside the head instead and cost nothing.
_clips:
fps is the tick rate; a frame can occupy several ticks with `@frame hold=N` in the .txt, which is where each clip's rhythm lives. Read the comment at the top of each file -- it says what the rhythm is for.

M7.1, variants: a clip entry may add `trigger` and `weight`, and both are optional. A clip with no `trigger` answers to its own name, which is what every entry below did before the field existed -- so nothing here changes meaning by the field being available. Clips that name the same `trigger` form a set, and asking for that name plays one of them: `wake` now means 'either entrance', while `wake_slide` still means exactly that drawing, so a script or --clip can reach one variant on purpose. The chooser never plays the same variant twice running when there is an alternative, and `weight` (default 1) makes one variant likelier than another -- with only two behind a trigger they must alternate, so weights start mattering at three.

The rule variants owe each other: same grid, and a one-shot must end on the drawing the clip that follows it starts from. Both entrances end on idle.txt's first frame.

M2.3c, the exit: `depart` is the leaving trigger, with `depart_fling` behind it, and the band is held on screen for as long as the longest variant takes. An exit is the entrance contract read backwards and it binds both ends -- first frame is idle.txt's first frame, so the cut into it from whatever was playing is no larger than a tick of idle; last frame is *empty*, because a one-shot holds its last drawing and an exit that ended on a body would be leaving the alpha fade to erase it. See the comment at the top of depart.txt.
_sprites: Accessories, drawn outside the body. offset is in cells from the anchor cell to the sprite's own top-left and may be negative. The union of the body and every placement here fixes the scale, so a placement is a cost whether the sprite is showing or not. Every one of these sits to the right of the head at y >= 0: the envelope comes out 22x16, the band takes 22 cells across at scale 16 with pixels to spare, and the body stays the full 256 px. Which clip turns which sprite on is M2.4's business, not the format's.

sprites.name: muted
sprites._about: Not a clip accessory like the four below it: this one is switched on by the panel when Claude's voice is muted and the chat is closed, and it outranks whatever the current clip would otherwise have put up. Seven wide at offset 2 instead of six at offset 3 -- same right edge, so the envelope is unchanged at 22x16 and the body keeps its full 256 px; the extra cell is what lets the cross inside the bubble read at all.
